Q: How to get sane definition of uint32_t when using newlib? A:

C standard does not specify which standard integer type uint32_t should alias to, or if it should alias to any standard type at all. Your assumption that uint32_t should be unsigned int is just that - an assumption. It holds true for gcc/glibc combo; it doesn't for gcc/newlib combo because newlib maps uint32_t to __UINT32_TYPE__ which is defined in gcc to be unsigned long for 32-bit newlib targets. You'd need to patch gcc or newlib to make it into int.

This is a very common mistake to make (e.g. I very recently saw llvm build issue because of their usage of std::max on int32_t and int arguments) but mistake nonetheless. Can't assume uint32_t is unsigned int, can't assume it can be losslessly converted to unsigned int (after all, int can be 16 bit), gotta use correct format specifiers. Like said in the comment, PRIx32 macro is the only correct specifier for uint32_t. Alternatively one could do an explicit conversion to unsigned long, and print that converted value instead.

EDIT: You are insistant you may use '%x' because uint and uint32_t happens to be same width on your particular target. Well no you may not, not according to C standard. '%x' is defined as:

The unsigned int argument is converted to ... unsigned hexadecimal notation (x or X)

%x implies unsigned int and nothing else. This is a singular type you may use. Anything else is not a valid C code; it might work on your target but it won't on another. Details of your particular target are not important. Like @user2357112 said uint32_t is no different from long in this matter - that's NOT unsigned int and can't be used. The compiler correctly warns you that your code is not a standard-compliant C code.

If you want to use '%x' with uint32_t... well, its your code. Use it. You could patch gcc/newlib to make uint32_t alias to unsigned int (I think this is the place to do it - https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/blob/master/gcc/config/newlib-stdint.h#L38), or you could just switch that warning off. Regardless of that your code would still be violating C standard (though it would work just fine as long as you stick to common 32/64 targets).

Q: Efficiently generate all unique 4-integer ratios within a range up to scaling A:

  1. Calculate all the primes up to and including half of your range, and their indices.

  2. Make a "Boolean" bit array "primes" of size [range][prime count].

  3. For each integer in your range, calculate if it is divisable by each prime, and if so, mark that boolean/bit as true/1. (Numbers should not be marked as multiples of themselves, or 1)

  4. Now you finally iterate over the combinations. For each combination, look up the primes array for each of the values. If any index in that array is true/1 for all of the values, then all the values in this combination are a multiple of that prime, and thus of another combination, and thus can be skipped.

Values up to ~625 would only have to calculate up to 64 primes, and thus each integers' primes row fits in a 64-bit integer, taking about 5kb total. 128 bits gets you ranges up to ~1417, about 23kb. You can very slightly increase the range by hard coding the "divisible by 2" check, but the range increases by such a small amount that it's not worth the performance penalty.

Q: SQL Server INSERT-OUTPUT including column from other table A:

You can abuse a MERGE statement to allow the referencing of the source table in the OUTPUT clause

DECLARE @mapping TABLE (
    DestId int,
    SourceId int
);

MERGE INTO dest_table AS T 
USING src_table1 AS S ON 1=0 -- false predicate will ALWAYS not match!
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN 
    INSERT (column1, column2) 
    VALUES (S.column1, S.column2) 
    OUTPUT inserted.id as DestID, S.id AS SourceID INTO @mapping
;

the trick is the 1=0 in the merge predicate forcing it to always use the INSERT WHEN NOT MATCHED clause of the MERGE.

I realise the question explicitly discounts the use of MERGE due to SQL-2005 being in use, however I thought the trick outlined in the answer by user212514 to be interesting enough to record here.

Q: How to represent template-based strong ID types, type aliases, and data structures in a UML class diagram? A:

For the design the implementation details do not always matter. So if you're not generating code (or create diagrams from code) then in the overall diagrams. I would just model them as a Data Type (not templated). And for clarity you might make one small diagram explaining how you derive those types from your template.
